summary: A slightly annotated list of the 100 RFCs from RFC 700 through RFC 799, serving as a status report on them. It is a handy index to that stretch of the series.

plainLanguage.summary: A table of contents with short notes for one hundred earlier memos, so people could see what had been written.

questions: how to find early internet protocols
what was on the internet in 1982
subtitle: An annotated index to 100 RFCs from the early internet era, 1980-1982.

tldr.problem: By 1982, the RFC series had grown to include hundreds of documents. Engineers needed a way to quickly find and understand the key RFCs in one stretch of the series.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 800 provides a brief summary of each RFC from number 700 through 799, listing the author, date, and a one or two sentence description of what each document covers.
tldr.outcome: It serves as a status report and reference guide for that hundred-RFC span, making it easier to navigate the growing series.

today: RFC 800 is an Informational document, a historical snapshot. It is not a standard itself, and many of the RFCs it summarizes have been updated or obsoleted. For anyone studying the early Internet or tracking the evolution of TCP/IP, it remains a useful finding aid.

sections.title: What This RFC Is
sections.content:
RFC 800 is a slightly annotated list of 100 RFCs, from RFC 700 through RFC 799. It functions as a status report on those documents, giving readers a bird's-eye view of what was published during that period. Each entry includes the RFC number, the author's name, the date, the title, and a brief note about the content.

This kind of summary document became a useful tool in the early RFC series. As the number of documents grew, readers needed a way to discover which ones were relevant without reading through every page.
sections.plainLanguage: This paper is a list of a hundred earlier papers, with short notes about what each one says. You can use it to find papers about topics you care about.

sections.title: The RFCs Covered: 700-799
sections.content:
The RFC series numbered 700 to 799 spans the period from 1979 to 1982, a formative time for the ARPANET and early Internet. The documents in this range address fundamental technologies: TCP and UDP, IP routing, Telnet and terminal protocols, mail systems, and network management. They also include less formal documents: meeting notes, surveys of which hosts support which protocols, and discussions of emerging problems like network congestion and security.

Some RFCs in this range obsolete earlier ones (for example, RFC 793 replaced RFC 761 as the TCP specification), documenting the gradual refinement of core standards.
sections.plainLanguage: These a hundred papers from 1979 to 1982 cover everything people were building for the internet: mail, file transfer, remote terminals, and how to route data around networks.

sections.title: Core Topics You'll Find
sections.content:
The RFCs listed in RFC 800 fall into a few major categories. Core protocols include TCP (RFC 793), UDP (RFC 768), ICMP (RFC 792), and IP (RFC 791)—the essential protocols still in use. Application protocols cover Telnet (RFC 764), FTP (RFC 765), SMTP (RFC 788), and the Domain Name System proposal (RFC 799). The range also includes administrative and planning documents: assigned numbers registries, protocol standards discussions, and implementation notes.

The annotations in RFC 800 are terse but informative, often noting whether a document revises an earlier RFC or points readers toward a newer version. This makes the document useful both as a historical record and as a guide to which specifications were current at that time.
sections.plainLanguage: The papers cover how to send data reliably, how to send quick messages without guarantees, how to look up names, and how to run a mail service. Some papers say 'don't use the old one anymore, use this new one instead.'

sections.title: A Snapshot of Protocol Development
sections.content:
RFC 800 captures a moment when the TCP/IP protocols were solidifying into their final early form. References within the document point to replaced standards: RFC 777 and 760 are both older versions that RFC 792 (ICMP) and RFC 791 (IP) supersede. This reflects the way the Internet Standards process works: early drafts circulate, discussion happens, and revised versions are published.

The RFCs included also show the breadth of work happening across ARPANET: not just protocols themselves, but the infrastructure to support them—from 1822 interface specifications (for the ARPANET IMP-host connection) to attempts at graphics protocols and virtual terminals. By listing them all, RFC 800 serves both as an index and as a historical record of what was on people's minds in 1980-1982.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 800 shows what everyone was working on in 1980-1982. Some of it, like TCP and email, became hugely important. Some of it, like some of the graphics proposals, didn't catch on.

sections.title: Using This Index
sections.content:
Readers encountering RFC 800 in 1982 or shortly after could use it as a finding aid: want to know about a new protocol for file transfer? Look up the 760s and 770s for FTP, and RFC 800 would point you to RFC 765. Unsure whether an old specification is still current? The annotations often note when a newer version exists.

For later readers, RFC 800 is primarily a historical reference. It shows what was considered important enough to document at that point in the Internet's development, and the entry for each RFC is often more concise than opening the full document. It remains useful for historians, implementers tracing the evolution of standards, and anyone curious about what the early Internet looked like.
sections.plainLanguage: In 1982, you could use this to find papers about topics you needed. Today it's like looking at a snapshot of what people cared about forty years ago.
